doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Pensacola musicians, Sunday dances and college bands
summary: Johnson names musicians from Pensacola and describes Sunday-night dances with visiting New Orleans bands and the importance of college bands.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: It seems to me I’ve heard about some other fine musicians who came out of that high school.

Oh sure. About I would say, roughly about ten. For a small town like that, if I may I’ll name some. The concert pianist Don Shirley; Junior Cook, a famous jazz saxophonist; and Gigi Gryce, one of the founders of bebop; well myself. Then we’ve had a fine bunch of musicians, white musicians, one was Tony Bruno, a famous trumpet player, he came out of Pensacola; and then we had Ray Brown was born there, Ray Brown, the famous bass player. So I would say about ten. And one of the, I’ll never be able to reason why because people, during the time I was a kid, people didn’t have a place to go. The only place to go was like Sunday night dances. And Pensacola was one of the few towns on the Gulf Coast that had dances, big bands, like on Sunday night. And it somehow got around that they had two — east side, like any other small town, they had an east side and a west side. And one side of the town was more sedate than the other, and they had two or three different bands. But the bands from New Orleans like Papa Celestin, Don Alberts, a great band from Houston, Texas, from New Orleans, and most all of the bands from around New Orleans, they paid a visit on Sunday night. Now I have to tell you that admission was twenty cents.

And things were so rough during those days, people saved up twenty cents to go hear a band. Then we had the college bands. The college bands, Alabama State Collegians which became the Erskine Hawkins Orchestra, and which became a place where I spent most of my life, the best years of my life, recording years. Then we had some bands from Florida A&M College. In other words, during those days the college bands was the thing, because there was only, a kid didn’t have to have a scholarship, all he could do is play, play great and have a big name you know all over the south and the next thing, the dean and everyone was likely trying to get this guy, because you remember that Erskine Hawkins, from Alabama State Teachers College, then as we know, we know where the Adderley brothers came from, Florida A&M. Then we had, further up north, we had the Duke Blue Devils, now you know who they were, that was Les Brown. Then we had Kay Kyser from the University of North Carolina. In other words having bands was the big thing in colleges during those days. I don’t know now, I read Down Beat and different magazines and things like that and I see where they’re having college bands contests and all of that.
They’re more for concerts, not dancing though.
They’re more for concerts and not dances.
